title: Artificial Intelligence
blurb: How machines learn and what's really inside a chatbot, explained without maths homework.

lessons.title: How machines learn
lessons.summary: No magic: examples, a lot of simple maths and millions of small corrections.

cards.title: Learning from examples, not rules
cards.text:
Try writing rules that recognise a cat: pointy ears, whiskers… but foxes have those too, and some cats hide their ears. You'd never finish.

Machine learning flips it around. You show the computer thousands of labelled photos and let it work out the patterns itself. The result is called a model.

deep.x: Traditional software is explicit: a programmer writes rules ("if the amount is over €10,000, flag it"). Machine learning inverts that: you supply examples of inputs and desired outputs, and an optimisation process finds the rules, encoded as numbers in a model.
When ML wins

x: The rules are too many or too fuzzy to write down (recognising faces, speech)
The patterns change over time (fraud tactics, customer behaviour)
There's lots of historical data with known outcomes

deep.x: When rules still win

items.b: rules, must be exact and auditable

deep.x: A model is a function

Formally, a trained model is a mathematical function with many adjustable numbers (parameters). Training sets those numbers so that the function maps inputs to outputs as accurately as possible on examples.

deep.w: ML systems understand the world like humans
deep.r: They learn statistical patterns from data, which can work brilliantly or fail strangely

deep.x: The phrase "Software 2.0" (Andrej Karpathy, 2017) describes this shift: code written by optimisation rather than by hand.

cards.title: A neuron is a weighted vote
cards.text:
The building block of a neural network is tiny. It takes a few inputs, multiplies each by a weight (how much it matters), adds them up and says yes if the total is high enough.

Should you go to the beach? Sunny counts +3, weekend +2, rain −4. Stack millions of these little votes in layers and you get a network that can recognise faces or write text.

deep.x: An artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function. It's a loose caricature of a biological neuron, which fires when enough input signals arrive.
The beach example worked out
Sunny (1) × 3 + weekend (1) × 2 + rain (0) × −4 + bias (−2) = 3. Above zero, so "go to the beach". If it rains: 3 + 2 − 4 − 2 = −1, so stay home.

x: With rain: 3 + 2 − 4 − 2 = −1
→ stay home

deep.x: Activation functions
Without a non-linear "twist", stacking layers would collapse into one big linear sum. Activation functions add that twist.

items.b: on or off, the original perceptron

deep.x: From neurons to networks
Neurons are arranged in layers. Early layers detect simple patterns; later layers combine them into complex concepts. Modern networks have billions of weights.
The first artificial neuron model was proposed by Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts in 1943; Frank Rosenblatt built the "Perceptron" machine in 1958.

cards.title: Try it: be the neuron
cards.text: Switch the inputs on and off. The neuron adds up input × weight, plus a small bias of −2 (it needs a reason to go), and fires when the total is above zero.

deep.x: The widget lets you be the neuron's inputs. Notice three things as you play: inputs with big positive weights push towards "fire"; negative weights act as vetoes; and the bias sets how easily the neuron fires at all.
What training would do

In a real network, nobody sets these weights by hand. Training adjusts each weight slightly after every batch of examples, increasing weights that helped correct answers and decreasing those that misled.

steps: Output compared with the right answer

deep.x: Why one neuron isn't enough

A single neuron draws one straight line between "yes" and "no". Some problems, like XOR ("one or the other but not both"), can't be split by a single line. In 1969 Minsky and Papert highlighted this, helping trigger the first "AI winter". Multiple layers solve it.

items: can learn XOR and much more

deep.x: Every large AI model is, at bottom, billions of these simple weighted sums.

cards.title: Training means nudging
cards.text:
A new network starts with random weights and makes terrible guesses. Training repeats a simple loop: make a guess, measure how wrong it was, then nudge every weight a tiny bit in the direction that reduces the error.

Picture a ball rolling downhill into the valley of lowest error. Large models repeat this billions of times.

deep.x: Training minimises a loss function: a number measuring how wrong the model is on the training examples. Gradient descent computes, for every weight, which direction would reduce the loss, and moves each weight a small step that way.
Key ingredients

items.b: direction of steepest increase in loss
a small sample of examples per step

deep.x: Backpropagation

Backpropagation uses the chain rule from calculus to calculate gradients for all weights efficiently, layer by layer from the output backwards. Popularised in 1986 by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, it's the engine of deep learning.
The learning rate dilemma
Scale
Frontier language models are trained for months on thousands of specialised chips, processing trillions of tokens, with total compute in the range of 10²⁵ floating-point operations or more.
Modern optimisers like Adam adapt the step size for each weight automatically, which made training deep networks far more reliable.

cards.title: Memorising isn't learning
cards.text:
A model can fit its training examples perfectly and still be useless, like a student who memorised last year's exam answers. This is called overfitting.

The fix is to test on examples the model has never seen. If it does well there too, it has learned the real pattern rather than the noise.

deep.x: Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data's noise and quirks instead of the underlying pattern. It scores brilliantly on training examples and poorly on new ones. Underfitting is the opposite: too simple to capture the pattern at all.

items: great on train, bad on test

deep.x: Spotting it
Plot error on training and validation data as training proceeds. When training error keeps falling but validation error starts rising, the model has begun memorising.
Remedies

x: More (and more varied) training data
Simpler models or fewer features
Regularisation: penalising very large weights
Dropout: randomly switching off neurons during training
Early stopping: halt when validation error stops improving

deep.x: The bias–variance trade-off

items.b: overly sensitive to the training set, overfits

deep.x: Very large modern networks sometimes show "double descent": test error gets worse, then better again as models grow far beyond the point where they can memorise everything.

cards.title: Features: what the model looks at

steps: 120 m², 3 bedrooms, 2 km to the coast

cards.text:
A model never sees "a house". It sees numbers that describe it, called features: floor area, number of bedrooms, distance to the coast, year built.

Choosing good features used to be most of the work. Deep learning learns many of them by itself, but the idea stays the same: the model can only use what you give it.

deep.x: A feature is a measurable input. Good features capture information relevant to the target and are available reliably at prediction time.
Feature engineering

Before deep learning, teams spent most of their time crafting features: ratios, aggregates, time since last event. For tabular business data (sales, transactions), it's still crucial, and tree-based models like gradient boosting often beat deep learning there.
Data leakage
A classic error is using a feature that wouldn't exist at prediction time, such as "account closed date" to predict churn. The model looks amazing in testing and fails in production.

deep.r: Irrelevant or leaky features hurt accuracy and robustness

deep.x: Learned features
In deep networks, early layers learn edges and textures, later layers learn object parts and concepts: features discovered automatically from raw pixels or text.
The model can only be as good as the information its features carry.

cards.title: Train, validate, test
cards.text:
You split your data before training. The model learns from the training set, you tune settings on the validation set, and the test set stays locked away until the very end.

If you peek at the test set while building the model, your final score will be too optimistic.

deep.x: Splitting data simulates the future: you want to know how the model will perform on data it has never seen. A common split is about 70/15/15, though it varies with dataset size.
Cross-validation
With limited data, k-fold cross-validation rotates which part is held out, training k times and averaging the results for a more reliable estimate.
Time matters
For forecasting, split by time: train on the past, validate on later data. Random splits leak future information into training and give over-optimistic results.
Distribution shift
Even a well-tested model can degrade when the world changes: new products, new fraud tactics, a pandemic. Production models need monitoring and periodic retraining.
Kaggle competitions keep a "private leaderboard" test set hidden until the end, because teams who tune endlessly on the public set often drop in the final ranking.

cards.title: The simplest model: a straight line
cards.text:
With one feature, a model can be a line. It multiplies the input by a weight and adds a bias. Training finds the weight and bias that make the line fit the data best.

Neural networks are millions of these little sums stacked together, with a twist added between them.

deep.x: Linear regression fits y = w·x + b to data by choosing w and b to minimise the squared differences between predicted and actual values. It's centuries old (Legendre and Gauss, around 1805) and still widely used.

items.m: slope, how much y changes per unit of x

deep.x: Many features
With several features, it becomes y = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + b. Each weight shows how much the prediction changes when that feature increases by one unit, holding the others fixed: easy to interpret.

x: 100 m², 3 rooms

deep.x: Logistic regression
For yes/no outcomes, logistic regression squashes the linear sum into a probability between 0 and 1. It's a common baseline for credit scoring and churn.
Why start simple

x: Fast to train, easy to explain to regulators and managers
Gives a baseline to beat
Often surprisingly competitive on structured data

deep.x: A neural network is many linear models stacked with non-linear twists between them.

cards.title: More data often beats a cleverer algorithm
cards.text:
In many real problems, a simple model trained on a lot of good data outperforms a sophisticated model trained on a little. Google researchers called this "the unreasonable effectiveness of data" in 2009.

Quality matters as much as quantity: a million mislabelled examples teach the wrong lesson very confidently.

deep.x: In 2001 Banko and Brill showed that for a language task, simple algorithms improved steadily with more data, and the differences between algorithms shrank. In 2009 Google's Halevy, Norvig and Pereira wrote "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data".
Scaling laws

For large neural networks, researchers found smooth "scaling laws" (2020): performance improves predictably as you increase data, model size and compute together. This guided the race to bigger language models.
But quality matters

x: Label noise teaches wrong patterns
Duplicates distort the model and inflate test scores
Biased samples produce biased models
Curated, high-quality data can beat raw quantity, as later language models showed

deep.r: Raw data is cheap; clean, relevant, well-labelled data is what's valuable

deep.x: In business projects, most effort typically goes into finding, cleaning and understanding data, not modelling.

cards.title: A spam filter, step by step
cards.text:
Every incoming email is turned into features: words used, sender reputation, number of links. The model outputs a score between 0 and 1. Above a threshold, say 0.9, it goes to spam.

Choosing that threshold is a business decision: lower it and you catch more spam but lose more real emails.

deep.x: Spam filtering was one of the first mass-market ML applications. Early filters (2002, Paul Graham's "A Plan for Spam") used naive Bayes: estimating how likely each word is in spam versus legitimate email.
Thresholds and trade-offs
Measuring it

x: **Precision**: of emails flagged as spam, how many really were spam?
**Recall**: of all spam, how much did we catch?
Losing an important email is usually worse than seeing a spam, so filters favour precision

deep.x: An adversarial game
Spammers adapt: misspellings, images instead of text, hijacked accounts. Filters retrain continuously and combine ML with sender reputation, authentication (SPF, DKIM) and user reports.
Every business ML system involves the same choices: features, a score, a threshold and the cost of each kind of error.

quiz.q: What does a machine-learning model learn from?
options: The internet's search results at runtime
quiz.explain: It finds patterns in example data. Nobody writes the rules by hand.

quiz.q: Sunny (+3) and raining (−4), not a weekend, bias −2. Does the beach neuron fire?
quiz.explain: 3 − 4 − 2 = −3, which is below zero, so no.

quiz.q: A model scores 100% on its training data but badly on new data. That's…
quiz.explain: It memorised the examples instead of the general pattern.

quiz.q: What is the test set for?
options: A final, honest check on unseen data
quiz.explain: It is kept aside and only used once, so the score reflects new data.

lessons.title: How chatbots work
lessons.summary: What's really going on inside ChatGPT, Claude and friends.

cards.title: Text becomes tokens
cards.text:
Language models don't read letters or whole words. Text is chopped into tokens: common words stay whole, rarer ones are split into pieces. Each token is just a number to the model.

In English a token averages about ¾ of a word, which is why AI services price and limit usage in tokens.

deep.x: Tokenisers split text using a learned vocabulary, often via byte-pair encoding: start with characters, repeatedly merge the most frequent pairs until the vocabulary reaches, say, 100,000–200,000 tokens.
Rules of thumb

items.b: often ~20–40% more tokens than English for the same text

deep.x: Why it matters

x: **Cost**: APIs charge per input and output token
**Limits**: context windows are counted in tokens
**Quirks**: models can struggle to count letters in a word because they see tokens, not letters
**Languages**: less common languages and scripts often need more tokens, costing more

deep.x: The classic failure "how many r's are in strawberry?" happened because models see "straw" + "berry" as chunks, not individual letters.
Numbers are tokenised oddly too, which is one reason models can stumble on arithmetic without tools.

cards.title: It predicts the next word
cards.text:
At heart, a language model does one thing: given the text so far, it estimates how likely each possible next token is. It picks one, adds it to the text and repeats.

Trained on a huge amount of writing, that simple trick ends up capturing grammar, facts, styles and a surprising amount of reasoning.

deep.x: A language model outputs a probability distribution over its whole vocabulary for the next token. Generation is a loop: sample a token, append it, recompute probabilities, repeat. This is called autoregressive generation.
Example
For "The capital of Portugal is", the model might assign "Lisbon" 92%, "a" 3%, "Porto" 1% and tiny probabilities to thousands of others.
Why prediction leads to "understanding"

To predict text well across physics papers, legal contracts, novels and code, the model must internalise grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and even models of the people writing. Whether that counts as understanding is debated, but the capabilities are real and measurable.
Reasoning models
Since 2024, "reasoning" models are trained to generate long chains of intermediate thinking before answering, which greatly improves maths, coding and planning.
Every response is built one token at a time; the model doesn't plan a whole paragraph in advance the way people often assume, though it does carry internal "intentions" forward.

cards.title: Try it: turn up the temperature
cards.text: Temperature controls how adventurous the model is. Low temperature almost always picks the top word; high temperature spreads the odds so rarer words get a chance. Press Generate a few times at each setting.

deep.x: Temperature rescales the model's probabilities before sampling. Low temperatures sharpen the distribution towards the most likely token; high temperatures flatten it, giving unlikely tokens a chance.
Which setting when?
Other sampling controls

x: **Top-k**: only consider the k most likely tokens
**Top-p (nucleus)**: only consider the smallest set of tokens adding up to probability p, e.g. 0.9
**Seed**: fixes randomness for reproducibility, where supported

deep.x: Temperature 0 isn't fully deterministic
Even at temperature 0, outputs can vary slightly between runs because of parallel computation on GPUs and batching. Don't rely on identical outputs without testing.

deep.w: Higher temperature makes the model smarter or more creative
deep.r: It only adds randomness; creativity comes from the prompt and the model

cards.title: Meaning as a map
cards.text:
Inside the model, every token becomes a list of numbers called an embedding, like coordinates on a map of meaning. Similar ideas sit close together: cat near dog, Lisbon near Porto.

Directions carry meaning too. The step from 'man' to 'woman' is roughly the same as from 'king' to 'queen'.

deep.x: An embedding is a vector, a list of hundreds to thousands of numbers, representing a token, word, sentence or document. Training places items that appear in similar contexts close together in this high-dimensional space.
Word arithmetic
In word2vec (2013), vector("king") − vector("man") + vector("woman") landed closest to vector("queen"). Directions encode relationships like gender, tense or country–capital.

x: king − man + woman
≈ queen
Paris − France + Portugal ≈ Lisbon

deep.x: Measuring similarity
Similarity is usually measured by cosine similarity: the angle between two vectors. 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated.
Business uses

x: Semantic search: find documents by meaning, not exact keywords
Retrieval for chatbots (RAG)
Recommendations, deduplication, clustering support tickets

deep.x: Embeddings are how machines turn messy meaning into geometry they can compute with.

cards.title: Fluent isn't the same as true
cards.text:
Because a model predicts plausible text, it can produce confident sentences that are simply wrong. People call this hallucination. It's most likely with exact numbers, dates, quotes and niche facts.

Use AI for drafting, explaining and brainstorming, and check anything important against a reliable source. (The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889.)

deep.x: Hallucination is when a model generates content that sounds plausible but is false or unsupported: invented citations, wrong figures, fake quotes. It arises because the training objective rewards plausible continuations, not verified truth.
High-risk areas
Reducing it

x: Ground answers in supplied documents (retrieval) and ask for citations
Let the model say "I don't know"; reward it in evaluation
Use tools: search, calculators, databases
Verify important outputs; use a second model or a human to check

deep.x: Famous incidents
In 2023 lawyers in New York were sanctioned for submitting a brief with case citations invented by a chatbot. Several similar cases followed worldwide.
Newer models hallucinate much less on common facts, but rates on obscure details remain significant, so verification is still essential.

cards.title: The context window
cards.text:
A model can only "see" a limited amount of text at once, measured in tokens. This is its context window: your question, the conversation so far and any documents you pasted.

When a conversation grows past the limit, the oldest parts are dropped or summarised. Windows have grown enormously since 2022.

deep.x: The context window is the model's working memory: everything it can attend to when producing the next token, including system instructions, conversation history, documents and its own output so far.
Bigger isn't the whole story

x: Cost and latency grow with the amount of context processed
Models can be worse at using information buried in the middle of very long contexts ("lost in the middle")
Retrieval (fetching only relevant pieces) is often cheaper and more accurate than stuffing everything in

deep.x: Memory across chats
A model doesn't remember previous conversations by itself. Products add "memory" by storing notes or summaries and inserting them into the context of new conversations.
Think of the context window as the desk the model works on: everything it needs must be on the desk.

cards.title: Pre-training, then fine-tuning

steps: Read vast text, predict next token

cards.text:
First the model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next token. That makes it knowledgeable but not yet helpful.

Then it is fine-tuned on examples of good answers, and trained further with human (and AI) feedback on which responses are better. That is what turns a text predictor into an assistant.

deep.x: Building an assistant happens in stages. Pre-training on trillions of tokens produces a "base model" that continues text. Post-training turns it into a helpful, honest, safe assistant.

steps: Pre-training: predict next token on huge text

deep.x: RLHF

Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people compare pairs of responses; a reward model learns their preferences; the language model is then optimised to produce responses the reward model rates highly. Popularised by InstructGPT (2022).

items.b: AI feedback guided by written principles

deep.x: Reinforcement learning on tasks
Newer pipelines also train models with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, such as maths problems and code with tests, which produces the long step-by-step reasoning of "reasoning models".
A base model asked "What is the capital of France?" might continue with more quiz questions instead of answering, because that's how such text often continues online.

cards.title: Better prompts, better answers

items: Give context: who it's for and why
Ask for a format: table, bullets, length

cards.text: The model only knows what you tell it. Say who you are, what you need, what good looks like and in what format. Paste the relevant data instead of describing it. If the first answer is off, say what to change.

deep.x: A prompt is the model's entire briefing. Vague prompts get generic answers. Good prompts give context, the goal, constraints and examples.
Before and after

items.r: "Write a 120-word LinkedIn post for CFOs about how our tool cuts month-end close by 2 days, confident, no hype, end with a question"

deep.x: Useful techniques

x: **Give examples** (few-shot): show two or three samples of the desired output
**Ask for reasoning** on complex problems, or use a reasoning model
**Structure inputs** with headings or tags so the model knows what's what
**Iterate**: treat the first answer as a draft and give specific feedback

deep.x: A useful test: would a smart new colleague be able to do the task well from your prompt alone?

cards.title: Models don't look things up by themselves
cards.text:
A plain language model answers from what it learned during training, which stops at a cutoff date. It doesn't know today's news or your files.

Modern assistants are given tools: web search, document access, code execution. With tools, they can fetch fresh facts instead of guessing.

deep.x: A model's built-in knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff and is fuzzy on details. Tool use lets the model request actions, like searching, querying a database or running code, and read the results before answering.

steps: Model decides it needs a tool

deep.x: Common tools

items.b: take actions, e.g. book, send, update

deep.x: Function calling

Developers describe tools with names and parameters; the model outputs a structured request like `get_weather(city="Porto")`, the application runs it and feeds back the result. Standards such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) make tools reusable across apps.
Risks
Tools add power and risk: a model reading a malicious web page could be manipulated by hidden instructions ("prompt injection"). Permissions and human approval for sensitive actions matter.
Agents are essentially models running in a loop: think, call a tool, observe, repeat, until the task is done.

cards.title: What "70B" means
cards.text:
Model sizes are counted in parameters, the learned weights. A 70B model has 70 billion of them. Stored in 16-bit format, each weight takes 2 bytes, so the model alone needs about 140 GB of memory.

That's why big models run in data centres, and why smaller or compressed (quantised) models run on laptops.

deep.x: Parameters are the learned numbers in a model. Their count roughly indicates capacity, though training data, architecture and post-training matter as much.
Quantisation
Storing weights with fewer bits shrinks models with modest quality loss. A 4-bit version of a 70B model fits in about 35–40 GB, possible on a high-end workstation.
More than weights
Running a model also needs memory for the "KV cache" holding the context being processed, which grows with context length and the number of simultaneous users.
Mixture of experts
Many recent models use a mixture-of-experts design: the total parameter count is large, but only a fraction is active for each token, cutting compute per token.

items: only a few "experts" active per token

deep.r: Smaller, well-trained or specialised models often match bigger ones on specific tasks at far lower cost

quiz.q: What does a language model actually do at each step?
options: Looks the answer up in a database
Predicts the most likely next token
quiz.explain: It estimates probabilities for the next token, picks one, and repeats.

quiz.q: Roughly how many English words fit in 1,000 tokens?
quiz.explain: A token averages about ¾ of a word in English.

quiz.q: You want consistent, predictable answers. Which temperature?
quiz.explain: Low temperature concentrates the odds on the most likely tokens.

quiz.q: Why might a chatbot not know about yesterday's news?
options: Its knowledge stops at a training cutoff unless it has a search tool
quiz.explain: Without tools, a model only knows what was in its training data.

lessons.title: Three ways machines learn
lessons.summary: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and when each fits.

cards.title: Supervised learning
cards.text:
You give the model examples with the right answers attached: photos labelled "cat" or "dog", houses with their sale price. It learns to map inputs to answers.

It's the most common kind of machine learning in business: forecasting, fraud detection, document classification.

deep.x: Supervised learning learns a mapping from inputs to known outputs using labelled examples. It's like learning with an answer key.
Everyday examples

items.b: how many units will sell next week?
does this scan show a fracture?

deep.x: Common algorithms

x: Linear and logistic regression: simple, interpretable baselines
Decision trees and random forests: handle mixed data well
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM): often best for tabular business data
Neural networks: best for images, audio, text

deep.x: The catch
Supervised learning learns what the past looked like. If labels reflect past biases or the world changes, the model will reproduce yesterday's patterns.
Ask early: do we have enough reliable historical outcomes to learn from?

cards.title: Classification vs regression
cards.text: Supervised problems come in two flavours. Classification picks a category: spam or not, which product type, which disease. Regression predicts a number: tomorrow's price, delivery time, energy demand.

deep.x: Both are supervised; the difference is the type of output.
Measuring each
Binary, multi-class, multi-label

x: **Binary**: two classes (fraud or not)
**Multi-class**: one of many (which of 50 product categories)
**Multi-label**: several at once (an article tagged "finance" and "energy")

deep.x: Turning one into the other

You can turn regression into classification by binning ("demand high/medium/low") and get probabilities from classifiers that behave like scores. The choice should follow the business decision being made.
Many "classification" models output probabilities; the final yes/no depends on a threshold you choose based on costs.

cards.title: Unsupervised learning
cards.text:
Here there are no labels. The model looks for structure on its own: groups of similar customers, unusual transactions, topics in a pile of documents.

It's useful when you don't yet know what you're looking for, or labelling would be too expensive.

deep.x: Without labels, the goal is to discover structure: groups, unusual points, compact representations. It's exploratory and often feeds later supervised work.

items: Topic modelling: find themes in text

deep.x: Typical algorithms

items.b: finds dense clusters of any shape
compresses many features into a few

deep.x: Anomaly detection in practice
Banks and factories use it to spot transactions or sensor readings unlike the norm, without needing examples of every possible fraud or failure.
Evaluating without labels
There's no answer key, so success is judged by whether results are stable, interpretable and useful: do the groups make business sense? Do flagged anomalies lead to real findings?
Unsupervised learning finds patterns; humans still decide whether they mean anything.

cards.title: Clustering customers
cards.text:
Give a clustering algorithm the purchase history of 100,000 customers and ask for five groups. It might find bargain hunters, weekend shoppers, big occasional buyers and so on.

The algorithm finds the groups; a human still has to look at them and decide what they mean.

deep.x: k-means clustering assigns each customer to the nearest of k centre points, then moves each centre to the average of its customers, repeating until stable. Features might include spend, visit frequency, recency and product categories.
RFM segmentation
A classic retail approach scores customers by Recency, Frequency and Monetary value, then clusters them.

items.b: used to buy often, not lately

deep.x: Choosing k
Too few clusters hide important differences; too many become unmanageable. Analysts use the "elbow method" (where adding clusters stops helping much) and, above all, business judgement.
From clusters to action

x: Tailored offers for each segment
Retention campaigns for "at risk" customers
Different service levels or channels

deep.x: Features must be scaled before clustering; otherwise a feature measured in euros will overwhelm one measured in visits.

cards.title: Reinforcement learning
cards.text:
An agent learns by trial and error. It takes an action, the environment responds, and it receives a reward or penalty. Over millions of attempts it learns which actions lead to the most reward.

This is how computers learned to play Go, chess and video games better than humans.

deep.x: In reinforcement learning (RL), an agent interacts with an environment, receiving rewards. It learns a policy, a rule for choosing actions, that maximises total future reward, balancing exploration (trying new things) with exploitation (using what works).
Landmarks
Where it's used

x: Game-playing and simulations
Robotics: learning to walk and grasp, often in simulation first
Data-centre cooling optimisation
Training language models with human feedback and on verifiable tasks

deep.x: Hard parts

items.b: which earlier action earned the reward?

deep.x: A boat-racing RL agent once learned to spin in circles collecting points forever instead of finishing the race: a famous example of reward hacking.

cards.title: Self-supervised learning
cards.text:
A clever trick: create the labels from the data itself. Hide a word in a sentence and ask the model to guess it. Hide part of an image and ask it to fill in the gap.

No humans needed to label anything, so you can train on billions of examples. Large language models are trained this way.

deep.x: Self-supervised learning creates training signals from the data itself: predict the next word, a masked word, a missing image patch, or whether two views come from the same image. This unlocks the internet's unlabelled data.
Why it was a breakthrough

Labelled datasets top out at millions of examples; unlabelled text and images run into trillions. Self-supervised pre-training lets models learn general representations at that scale, then adapt to specific tasks with few labels.
Foundation models
Models pre-trained this way are called foundation models: one general model adapted to countless tasks through prompting or fine-tuning.
Yann LeCun called self-supervised learning "the cake", with supervised learning the icing and RL the cherry.

cards.title: Labels are expensive
cards.text:
Supervised learning needs labelled data, and labelling is slow human work. Medical images need doctors; legal documents need lawyers.

That cost is why self-supervised pre-training became so important: learn general knowledge from unlabelled data first, then fine-tune with a small labelled set.

deep.x: Labelling requires time, expertise and consistency. Medical image labels may cost tens of euros each; complex legal or engineering annotations far more. Disagreement between labellers adds noise.
Ways to reduce cost

x: **Pre-train, then fine-tune**: needs far fewer labels
**Active learning**: the model picks the most informative examples for humans to label
**Weak supervision**: use rules and heuristics to generate noisy labels
**LLM-assisted labelling**: a model proposes labels, humans review

deep.x: Label quality
Clear guidelines, examples, double-labelling and measuring agreement between labellers make a big difference. Bad labels quietly cap a model's accuracy.

deep.r: Labels are human judgements and can be inconsistent or biased

cards.title: Semi-supervised: a little help goes far
cards.text: Often you have a few labelled examples and a mountain of unlabelled ones. Semi-supervised methods use the labelled ones to get started, then let the model label the rest, keeping only its confident guesses.

deep.x: Semi-supervised learning combines a small labelled set with a large unlabelled one. A common technique, pseudo-labelling, trains on labelled data, predicts labels for unlabelled data, keeps only confident predictions, and retrains.
Why it works
Unlabelled data shows the shape of the data: where natural clusters and boundaries lie. Decision boundaries should pass through sparse regions, not cut through dense clusters.
Risks
If the model's early guesses are wrong but confident, it can reinforce its own mistakes ("confirmation bias"). Careful thresholds and validation on genuine labels are essential.

x: Works best when unlabelled data comes from the same distribution as labelled data
Common in speech recognition and document classification

deep.x: In practice, many teams now start from a pre-trained foundation model, which achieves similar benefits more easily.

cards.title: Which approach fits?

viz.root: Do you have the right answers?

cards.text: Have past examples with known outcomes? Supervised. Want to discover structure? Unsupervised. Is it a sequence of decisions with a goal, like a game or a robot? Reinforcement.

deep.x: Pick the approach from the problem and the data you have, not from the latest headline.

items: Want hidden groups or anomalies? Unsupervised
Language or images at scale? Pre-trained foundation model

deep.x: Questions to ask first

items: What data do we have, with what labels?

deep.x: Combinations are common
A fraud system might cluster transactions (unsupervised), flag anomalies, then use a supervised model trained on confirmed fraud, with an LLM summarising cases for investigators.
Sometimes the best "AI" solution is a well-designed rule or a dashboard; reaching for ML first is a common mistake.

cards.title: Most business AI is supervised
cards.text: Despite the headlines about game-playing and chatbots, most deployed machine learning in companies is still supervised: predicting churn, demand, defaults or delays from historical records.

deep.x: Surveys of enterprise AI consistently find classic predictive models in production far outnumber reinforcement learning. Generative AI has grown rapidly since 2023, but much of the measurable value still comes from forecasting, scoring and classification.
Why supervised dominates

x: Businesses already have historical records with outcomes
Results are measurable against known answers
Models can be audited and explained

deep.x: Where GenAI adds

Generative models increasingly sit alongside predictive ones: extracting fields from documents to feed models, explaining scores in plain language, or drafting responses. In commodity trading, for example, an LLM might read contracts while a forecasting model predicts prices.
The biggest returns usually come from improving a core decision that's made thousands of times a day.

quiz.q: Predicting tomorrow's electricity demand in kWh is…
quiz.explain: A number is being predicted, so it's regression.

quiz.q: An AI that learns chess by playing millions of games against itself uses…
quiz.explain: It learns from wins and losses, which are rewards.

quiz.q: Hiding a word in a sentence and asking the model to guess it is…
quiz.explain: The data provides its own labels.

lessons.title: Data: the fuel
lessons.summary: Where training data comes from and how it goes wrong.

cards.title: Garbage in, garbage out
cards.text:
A model is a summary of its training data. If the data is wrong, incomplete or skewed, the model will be too, and it will be wrong with great confidence.

In real projects, preparing data usually takes more time than building the model.

deep.x: A model compresses the patterns in its training data. Errors, gaps and biases in that data become errors, gaps and biases in the model, often hidden behind a confident score.
Typical data problems
Data quality dimensions

x: **Accuracy**: does it reflect reality?
**Completeness**: are key fields filled?
**Consistency**: same meaning across systems?
**Timeliness**: up to date when needed?
**Lineage**: do we know where it came from?

deep.x: In enterprise systems

In ERP landscapes like SAP, master data (customers, materials, vendors) often has duplicates and inconsistent codes across plants or countries. Cleaning and governing master data is often the hidden first project of any AI initiative.

items: each team fixes data its own way

deep.x: A small, clean dataset usually beats a large, dirty one.

cards.title: Data work dominates projects
cards.text: Surveys of data scientists consistently find that collecting, cleaning and organising data takes the largest share of their time. Training the model is often the quick part.

deep.x: Data preparation includes finding the right sources, getting access, joining tables, fixing quality issues, building features and documenting it all. Practitioners commonly estimate it at well over half of project effort.
Why it takes so long

x: Data sits in many systems with different owners and definitions
Access approvals for personal or sensitive data take time
Business rules ("what counts as an active customer?") must be agreed
Historical data reflects old processes that have since changed

deep.x: Making it faster
The deployment gap

Many ML prototypes never reach production. Industry surveys have long reported that a large share of models stall between pilot and deployment, usually because of data pipelines, integration and ownership, not algorithms.
Teams that invest in data foundations once often find later AI projects take weeks instead of months.

cards.title: Structured vs unstructured data
cards.text:
Structured data fits in tables: transactions, sensor readings, ERP records. Unstructured data is everything else: emails, contracts, photos, audio.

Classic machine learning loves tables. Deep learning made unstructured data usable at scale.

deep.x: Estimates suggest around 80% of enterprise data is unstructured: emails, PDFs, contracts, images, chat logs. Until recently, most of it was effectively unusable for analytics.
Different tools
Semi-structured
JSON, XML, logs and EDI messages sit in between: they have tags or fields but flexible structure. Trading confirmations and logistics messages are often semi-structured.
LLMs change the picture

Large language models can turn unstructured text into structured fields: extracting contract terms, counterparties, quantities, prices and dates from PDFs into tables, which then feed classic analytics.
Unlocking unstructured documents is one of the highest-value uses of generative AI in business.

cards.title: Missing values
cards.text:
Real data has gaps: a sensor went offline, a field was left empty. You can drop those rows, fill them with an average, or let the model treat "missing" as information in itself.

Sometimes the fact that a value is missing says something, like a customer who never gave a phone number.

deep.x: Missing data is common and rarely random. How you handle it can change results significantly.

items: Missing completely at random: sensor glitch
Missing at random: related to other known data
Missing not at random: related to the missing value itself

deep.x: Options

items.b: simple, but loses data and may bias

deep.x: Missing can be informative
A loan applicant who leaves "employer" blank, or a machine whose temperature sensor stopped reporting, may be telling you something. Adding a "was missing" indicator often improves models.
Tree models handle it
Gradient-boosting libraries like XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values natively, learning which direction missing cases should go at each split.

deep.r: Zero may be a real, meaningful value; filling blindly can mislead the model

deep.x: Always ask why data is missing before deciding how to fill it.

cards.title: Data leakage

items.r: use only data known before the decision
split by date: past trains, future tests

cards.text:
Leakage happens when the training data contains information the model won't have when it's used for real. A churn model trained with a "cancellation date" column will look brilliant in testing and fail in production.

Always ask: would I know this value at the moment I make the prediction?

deep.x: Leakage occurs when information from outside the prediction moment sneaks into training. Test scores look excellent; real-world performance collapses.

items: Future data: using values recorded after the event
Target proxies: features derived from the answer
Train–test contamination: same records in both sets
Preprocessing leaks: scaling using the whole dataset

deep.x: Classic examples

items.b: uses "chargeback flag", only known after fraud

deep.x: How to prevent it

x: Build features "as of" the prediction time, using point-in-time snapshots
Split data by time for forecasting
Fit scalers and encoders on training data only
Be suspicious of any model that seems too good to be true

deep.x: In a famous case, a pneumonia-risk model learned that asthma patients had lower risk, because they were sent straight to intensive care: a correlation driven by treatment, not biology.

cards.title: Sampling bias
cards.text: If your data doesn't represent the people or situations the model will meet, it will fail on the ones it never saw. A face detector trained mostly on one group performs worse on others.

deep.x: Sampling bias happens when training data systematically differs from the population a model will serve. The model may work well for the majority and poorly for others.
Famous examples

x: In 2018 the "Gender Shades" study found commercial face-analysis systems had error rates under 1% for lighter-skinned men but up to about 35% for darker-skinned women
Speech recognisers trained mostly on certain accents performed worse on others
Models trained on one hospital's equipment struggled with another's scanners

deep.x: Survivorship bias
Training only on successful cases, like loans that were approved, hides how rejected applicants would have behaved. The model never learns about the people who were filtered out.
Fixes
Ask "who or what is missing from this dataset?" before trusting results.

cards.title: Data drift
cards.text:
The world changes and models trained on last year's data slowly go stale. Customer behaviour shifts, prices change, a new product appears.

That's why deployed models need monitoring and periodic retraining.

deep.x: Models assume the future resembles the training data. When the world shifts, performance decays, sometimes gradually, sometimes overnight.

items: Concept drift: relationship between inputs and outcome changes

deep.x: COVID-19: a global drift event

In March 2020, demand forecasting, fraud and credit models worldwide broke as shopping, travel and payment patterns changed abruptly. Many teams had to switch to simpler rules or retrain on weeks of new data.
Monitoring

x: Track input distributions against the training baseline
Track prediction distributions and, when available, actual outcomes
Set alerts and retraining triggers

deep.x: In commodities
Price and logistics models drift with weather, geopolitics, regulations and new trade routes; regular retraining and human oversight are standard practice.
Population Stability Index (PSI) is a common metric in banking to quantify how much a variable's distribution has drifted.

cards.title: Synthetic data
cards.text:
When real data is scarce or private, you can generate artificial examples: simulated sensor faults, fake but realistic invoices, rendered images.

It helps, but synthetic data only contains the patterns you put into it. Always test on real data.

deep.x: Synthetic data is generated rather than collected: by simulations, rules, or generative models trained on real data. Gartner and others predicted rapid growth in its use for AI training and testing.
Benefits

x: Privacy: no real individuals
Rare events: generate fraud or failure cases that seldom occur
Testing: realistic data for software without exposing production data

deep.x: Limits
Model collapse
Research has shown that training generative models repeatedly on their own outputs can degrade quality over generations: diversity shrinks and errors compound. Real data remains essential.
Synthetic data is a supplement, never a full replacement for real-world validation.

cards.title: Data and privacy

items: Keep a record of where it came from

cards.text:
Personal data used for training falls under laws such as the EU's GDPR. You need a legal basis, should collect only what's needed, and must protect it.

Anonymising data is harder than it looks: combining a few fields like postcode, birth date and gender can identify many people.

deep.x: The GDPR, in force since 2018, governs personal data in the EU. AI training, profiling and automated decisions all fall within its scope, and the EU AI Act adds AI-specific rules.
Re-identification
Latanya Sweeney showed in 2000 that about 87% of Americans could be uniquely identified by just ZIP code, birth date and gender. "Anonymous" datasets often aren't.
Privacy techniques

items.b: replace names with codes, still personal data
add statistical noise to protect individuals
train where data lives, share only updates

deep.x: Automated decisions

Under GDPR Article 22, people have rights regarding decisions based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects, such as credit refusals, including meaningful information about the logic involved.
Fines for GDPR breaches can reach €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

cards.title: Labelling quality
cards.text: Labels are created by people, and people disagree or make mistakes. Good projects write clear labelling guidelines, have several people label the same examples, and measure how often they agree.

deep.x: Labels are judgements. Two experts may disagree on whether a transaction is suspicious or an X-ray shows a fracture. Measuring and managing that disagreement is part of building a good dataset.
Agreement metrics
Cohen's kappa measures agreement beyond chance: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than chance. Values above about 0.8 are usually considered strong.
Practical tips

x: Include edge cases and counter-examples in guidelines
Use gold-standard items to check labeller quality
Track disagreements: they reveal unclear definitions
Re-label periodically as definitions evolve

deep.x: LLMs as labellers
Language models can pre-label text quickly, with humans reviewing. It speeds up work, but models can share systematic blind spots, so audit samples carefully.
If experts can't agree on a label, a model trained on it can't be better than that disagreement allows.

quiz.q: A model looks perfect in testing but fails in production. A likely cause is…
quiz.explain: Leakage gives the model information during training that it won't have in real use.

quiz.q: What is data drift?
options: The real world changing so old training data no longer matches
quiz.explain: Patterns shift over time, so models need monitoring and retraining.

quiz.q: Which is unstructured data?
quiz.explain: Text, images and audio don't fit neatly into rows and columns.

lessons.title: Classic algorithms
lessons.summary: The workhorses that still run much of business AI.

cards.title: Linear regression
cards.text:
The oldest trick: draw the best straight line through the data. It predicts a number from a weighted sum of the inputs.

It's fast, easy to explain ("each extra m² adds €2,500") and often a strong baseline before trying anything fancier.

deep.x: Linear regression finds weights that minimise the sum of squared differences between predictions and actual values (ordinary least squares). There's even a closed-form solution, no iterative training required for small problems.
Interpreting weights
Each weight is the expected change in the prediction for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding others constant. That makes linear models popular wherever decisions must be explained.

x: Rent = 300 + 9 × m² + 150 × near metro
70 m², near metro

deep.x: Assumptions and pitfalls

items.b: effects add up in straight lines
errors don't depend on each other
can pull the line a lot

deep.x: Regularised versions
Ridge and lasso regression add a penalty for large weights. Lasso can shrink unhelpful weights to exactly zero, selecting features automatically.
The term "regression" comes from Francis Galton's 1880s observation that children of very tall parents tend to be less extreme: "regression towards the mean".

cards.title: Logistic regression
cards.text:
Despite the name, it's for classification. It squeezes a weighted sum into a probability between 0 and 1 using an S-shaped curve. Above 0.5 means "yes".

Banks have used it for decades for credit scoring because every weight can be explained.

deep.x: Logistic regression computes a weighted sum, then passes it through the sigmoid function to get a probability between 0 and 1. It's trained by maximising the likelihood of the observed outcomes.
Odds and scorecards

Each weight changes the log-odds of the outcome. Credit scorecards convert these weights into points: e.g. "homeowner +25 points, missed payment −40 points", making decisions transparent and auditable.
Why it's still everywhere

x: Regulators and auditors can follow every step
Robust with modest data
Calibrated probabilities: a 20% score really means about 1 in 5

deep.x: The threshold
0.5 is just a default. A bank might reject only above 0.3 default risk, or above 0.1, depending on margins, risk appetite and regulation.
Many "AI" credit decisions in practice still rely on logistic-regression scorecards, sometimes enriched with ML features.

cards.title: Decision trees
cards.text:
A tree asks a series of yes/no questions: Is income above €30k? Has the customer missed a payment? Each path ends in a prediction.

Trees are easy to read and explain, but a single tree tends to overfit.

deep.x: A decision tree splits data with a sequence of questions chosen to make each resulting group as "pure" as possible. Algorithms like CART pick the split that most reduces impurity (Gini or entropy) at each step.

items: Income above €30k?: Yes: check missed payments

deep.x: Strengths

x: Easy to visualise and explain to non-specialists
Handle numbers and categories, little preparation needed
Capture interactions ("young AND renting AND new job")

deep.x: Weaknesses

x: A single deep tree overfits badly
Small data changes can produce a very different tree
Predictions are step-like, not smooth

deep.x: Pruning
Limiting depth or cutting back branches that don't improve validation accuracy controls overfitting.
Doctors have long used hand-made decision trees as clinical flowcharts; ML trees automate building them from data.

cards.title: Random forests
cards.text: Train hundreds of slightly different decision trees on random slices of the data, then let them vote. The crowd is far more accurate and stable than any single tree.

deep.x: A random forest, introduced by Leo Breiman in 2001, trains many trees on bootstrap samples (random samples with replacement) and considers only a random subset of features at each split. Averaging many decorrelated trees reduces variance dramatically.
Why randomness helps
If every tree saw the same data and features, they'd make the same mistakes. Randomness makes their errors different, so they cancel out when averaged: the wisdom of crowds.
Practical benefits

x: Strong results with little tuning
Built-in estimate of accuracy using "out-of-bag" samples
Feature importance scores to see what matters

deep.x: Limits

x: Large models can be slow to predict
Less accurate than gradient boosting on many tasks
Feature importance can be biased towards features with many values

deep.x: Random forests are a great "second model" after a linear baseline.

cards.title: Gradient boosting
cards.text:
Instead of trees voting independently, boosting builds them in sequence. Each new tree focuses on the mistakes of the ones before it.

Libraries like XGBoost and LightGBM win many competitions on tabular data and are widely used in industry.

deep.x: Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially. Each new tree is trained to predict the remaining errors (residuals) of the current ensemble, and its output is added with a small learning rate. Many weak trees combine into a strong model.

steps: Fit a small tree to errors

deep.x: Popular libraries

items.b: Microsoft, very fast on large data

deep.x: Where it dominates
Benchmarks on tabular datasets repeatedly find gradient-boosted trees matching or beating deep learning, especially on medium-sized data with heterogeneous features.
Key settings

x: Number of trees and learning rate (more trees, smaller steps)
Tree depth (interaction complexity)
Early stopping on validation data

deep.x: Explanation tools like SHAP values were widely adopted largely to explain gradient-boosted models in finance and healthcare.

cards.title: k-nearest neighbours
cards.text:
To classify something new, find the k most similar examples you already know and take a vote. A new house is priced like its five most similar neighbours.

Simple and intuitive, but slow when the dataset is huge.

deep.x: k-NN stores all training examples and, for a new case, finds the k closest ones by a distance measure, then votes (classification) or averages (regression). There's no training phase: it's "lazy learning".

steps: Measure distance to all known items

deep.x: Choosing k
Distance matters
Features must be scaled, or one measured in large numbers (salary in euros) dominates one in small numbers (years of experience). Choosing the right distance metric is key.
Modern relevance
The idea is everywhere in vector search: retrieving the most similar documents, products or images by embedding distance is nearest-neighbour search, accelerated by approximate algorithms like HNSW.
Real-estate "comparables", valuing a house from similar recent sales, is human k-nearest neighbours.

cards.title: k-means clustering
cards.text: An unsupervised classic. Pick k centre points, assign every item to its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its group, and repeat until nothing changes.

deep.x: k-means minimises the total squared distance between points and their assigned cluster centre. It's fast and scales to millions of points, but you must choose k, and results depend on the starting positions.
Limitations
Better starts
The k-means++ initialisation (2007) spreads the initial centres out, giving better and more consistent results. It's the default in most libraries.
Alternatives
Clustering output is a hypothesis about structure; validate it with domain experts.

cards.title: Deep learning isn't always best
cards.text:
For tables of numbers, such as sales, prices or sensor logs, gradient-boosted trees often match or beat neural networks, train faster and are easier to explain.

Neural networks shine with images, audio and text.

deep.x: On structured, tabular data, studies like Grinsztajn et al. (2022) found tree-based models still outperform deep networks on typical medium-sized datasets, while being faster to train and tune.
Why trees suit tables

x: Columns have different meanings and scales; trees don't care
Business data has sharp thresholds ("over 90 days late") that trees capture naturally
Irrelevant columns hurt neural nets more

deep.x: When deep learning helps with tables

x: Very large datasets
Mixing tables with text, images or sequences
Transfer from foundation models trained on many tables, an active research area

steps: Compare with a neural net if data is large

deep.w: Deep learning is always the most advanced choice
deep.r: The best model is the one that performs best on your data and constraints

cards.title: Start with a baseline
cards.text: Before building anything complex, measure a dumb baseline: "predict the average" or "same as last week". If your clever model barely beats it, it's not worth deploying.

deep.x: A baseline is the simplest reasonable prediction. It sets the bar any model must clear to justify its complexity and cost.

items.b: same as last week, or seasonal naive
always predict the most common class

deep.x: The accuracy trap

In fraud detection, if 99.5% of transactions are legitimate, a model that always says "legitimate" scores 99.5% accuracy while catching zero fraud. Always compare with the baseline and use metrics suited to the problem.
Business baselines
The real baseline is often the current human or rule-based process. A model must beat it on the metric that matters (cost, time, risk), including the cost of running and maintaining it.
In many forecasting competitions, simple statistical methods and their combinations have performed remarkably well against complex ones.

cards.title: Choosing an algorithm

items: What kind of data: table, text, image?

cards.text: Think about the data type, how much data you have, whether you must explain decisions, and how fast predictions need to be. In practice, teams try a few and pick by measured results.

deep.x: There's no universally best algorithm (the "no free lunch" theorem). Choice depends on data, constraints and the decision being supported.

items: Tabular, explainable? Logistic regression or small trees
Images, text, audio? Deep learning or foundation models
Few labels? Pre-trained models plus fine-tuning

deep.x: Constraints to weigh

items.b: milliseconds for payments vs hours for reports
who will retrain and monitor it?

deep.x: A practical process
Don't forget
Often, improving data quality or features gives a bigger jump than switching algorithms.
Model selection is an engineering decision, not a beauty contest.

quiz.q: Which method builds trees one after another, each fixing the previous ones' errors?
quiz.explain: Boosting is sequential; random forests are independent trees that vote.

quiz.q: Logistic regression is mainly used for…
quiz.explain: It outputs a probability for a yes/no outcome.

quiz.q: For a table of sales data, a strong first choice is often…
quiz.explain: Boosted trees are fast and accurate on tabular data.

lessons.title: Inside a neural network
lessons.summary: Layers, activations and how the network learns from its mistakes.

cards.title: Layers

steps: Hidden layers find edges, shapes, parts

cards.text:
A neural network is organised in layers. The input layer receives the data, hidden layers transform it step by step, and the output layer gives the answer.

"Deep" learning simply means many hidden layers.

deep.x: A feed-forward neural network passes data through layers of neurons. Each layer applies a matrix multiplication (weights), adds biases and applies an activation function. The output of one layer is the input to the next.
Width and depth
Why depth helps

Deep networks can represent complex functions much more efficiently than shallow ones, by building concepts hierarchically. But depth made training hard until techniques like ReLU, better initialisation, batch normalisation and residual connections arrived around 2010–2015.
Residual connections
ResNet (2015) added "skip connections" that let information bypass layers, enabling networks with 100+ layers. Transformers use them too.
The 2012 AlexNet, with 8 layers and 60 million parameters, kicked off the deep learning boom by winning ImageNet by a wide margin.

cards.title: Each layer learns more abstract features
cards.text:
In an image network, early layers detect edges and colours. Middle layers combine them into textures and shapes. Later layers recognise eyes, wheels or faces.

Nobody programs these features; they emerge from training.

deep.x: Visualising trained image networks shows a hierarchy: edges and colour blobs in the first layers, textures and simple shapes next, then parts (eyes, wheels) and finally whole objects.
Similar in language models
Research on language models finds early layers capture word pieces and syntax, middle layers capture meanings and relationships, and later layers prepare the next-token prediction.
Interpretability research

Mechanistic interpretability tries to reverse-engineer what individual neurons and circuits do. Researchers have found "features" for concepts such as specific places, code bugs or emotions inside large models.
Transfer learning
Because early layers learn generic features, a network trained on millions of photos can be fine-tuned for X-rays or crop disease with far less data.
Nobody programs these features: they emerge because they help reduce the training loss.

cards.title: Activation functions
cards.text:
Between layers, each neuron passes its sum through an activation function. The most common, ReLU, simply turns negative values into zero.

Without this non-linear step, stacking layers would collapse into one big straight-line model.

deep.x: Activation functions introduce non-linearity, letting networks model curved, complex relationships. Without them, any number of layers would equal a single linear transformation.
Why ReLU took over

Sigmoid and tanh flatten out for large inputs, so gradients become tiny and deep networks stop learning (the "vanishing gradient" problem). ReLU keeps gradients alive for positive values and is cheap to compute.
Output activations
ReLU's simplicity, just setting negatives to zero, was a surprisingly important ingredient in making deep learning practical.

cards.title: The loss function
cards.text:
To learn, the network needs a score for how wrong it is. That's the loss. For a price prediction, it might be the average squared error; for classification, how little probability it gave the right answer.

Training is the search for weights that make the loss as small as possible.

deep.x: The loss turns "how wrong is the model?" into a single number to minimise. Choosing it defines what the model optimises for, so it encodes business priorities.
Cross-entropy explained
If the correct class gets probability 0.9, the loss is small (−log 0.9 ≈ 0.1). If it gets 0.01, the loss is large (−log 0.01 ≈ 4.6). Confident mistakes are punished hardest.

v.unit: loss when true class gets probability p

deep.x: Language models
LLMs are trained with cross-entropy on the next token: minimising how surprised the model is by the actual next word across trillions of examples.
Business alignment
If under-forecasting stock costs more than over-forecasting, use an asymmetric loss (like quantile loss) instead of plain squared error.
Whatever you choose to minimise, the model will minimise; choose carefully.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.text:
After a wrong guess, the error is sent backwards through the network. Using calculus, each weight learns how much it contributed to the mistake and in which direction to move.

This algorithm, popularised in 1986, is how virtually every neural network is trained today.

deep.x: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in one backward sweep. Its cost is roughly the same as a couple of forward passes, which makes training billions of weights feasible.

steps: Forward pass: compute outputs and loss

deep.x: History
The idea appeared in several forms (Linnainmaa 1970, Werbos 1974), but Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams' 1986 paper showed it could train multilayer networks to learn useful internal representations.
Automatic differentiation
Frameworks like PyTorch and JAX compute gradients automatically: developers write the forward computation, and the framework derives the backward pass.
Vanishing and exploding gradients
In very deep networks, gradients can shrink to nothing or blow up as they pass back through layers. ReLU, careful initialisation, normalisation and residual connections tame this.
Geoffrey Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield for foundational work on neural networks.

cards.title: Learning rate
cards.text: How big should each nudge be? That's the learning rate. Too small and training takes forever. Too large and the model overshoots the valley and never settles.

deep.x: The learning rate sets the size of each weight update. It's often the single most important hyperparameter to tune.
Schedules
Training typically uses a warm-up (start small, increase), then gradually decreases the learning rate, for example with cosine decay. Big steps early explore; small steps late fine-tune.
Adaptive optimisers
Adam (2014) and AdamW adapt the effective step size for each weight based on recent gradients, making training more robust to the choice of learning rate.

items.b: Adam with better weight decay, standard for transformers

deep.x: Practitioners often run a quick "learning rate finder" sweep before full training.

cards.title: Batches and epochs
cards.text: Training data is fed in small batches, say 32 examples at a time, and the weights are updated after each batch. One full pass through all the data is an epoch. Networks often train for many epochs.

deep.x: Computing the gradient over all data at once is too slow; using one example at a time is too noisy. Mini-batches, typically 32 to thousands of examples, balance accuracy and speed, and fit GPU memory.

v.f: steps per epoch = dataset size ÷ batch size

deep.x: Terms

items.b: one pass through all training data

deep.x: Large models are different
Large language models often see each training token only about once: they train on so much data that a full second epoch isn't needed or would cause memorisation.

items: many epochs over the same data
about one pass over trillions of tokens

deep.x: Batch size effects

x: Larger batches: smoother gradients, better hardware use, may need higher learning rates
Smaller batches: noisier updates that can help generalisation

deep.x: Training frontier models uses batches of millions of tokens, spread across thousands of GPUs working in parallel.

cards.title: Dropout and regularisation

items: Early stopping: stop when validation stops improving

cards.text: To stop a network memorising, you can randomly switch off some neurons during training (dropout) or penalise very large weights. The network is forced to learn patterns that are robust, not fragile shortcuts.

deep.x: Regularisation discourages a model from fitting noise, improving generalisation. Dropout, introduced by Hinton's group in 2012–14, randomly zeroes a fraction of neurons during each training step, so the network can't rely on any single pathway.

steps: During training: randomly drop 10–50% of neurons

deep.x: Other techniques
Data augmentation for images
Flip, rotate, crop, change brightness or add noise to images. The model learns that a cat is still a cat in any of these variations.
Why it works
Dropout is like training a huge ensemble of thinned networks that share weights; at test time, using all neurons approximates averaging them.
Regularisation trades a little training accuracy for much better performance on new data.

cards.title: Convolutions in one picture

steps: Map of where the pattern appears

cards.text: A convolutional layer slides a small filter, say 3×3 pixels, across the image, looking for the same pattern everywhere: an edge, a curve, a texture. It's why image networks recognise a cat in any corner of the photo.

deep.x: A convolutional layer slides small learnable filters across an image. Each filter computes a weighted sum over a small patch, producing a "feature map" showing where its pattern appears. Using the same filter everywhere means far fewer parameters and translation-invariant detection.
Key ideas

items.b: how far it moves each step

deep.x: Landmark models
Still widely used
CNNs remain efficient for many vision tasks on phones and edge devices, such as defect detection on production lines and medical image analysis, though transformers now compete.
Yann LeCun's LeNet was used by US banks in the 1990s to read handwritten digits on millions of cheques.

cards.title: Why GPUs?

items: same sum on lots of data

cards.text: Training means multiplying huge grids of numbers, over and over. Graphics cards were built to do thousands of simple calculations in parallel for video games, which turned out to be exactly what neural networks need.

deep.x: Neural network training is dominated by matrix multiplications: huge numbers of independent multiply-and-add operations. CPUs have a few powerful cores; GPUs have thousands of simpler cores that do these in parallel.
History
In 2009–2012, researchers showed GPUs could speed up neural network training tens of times. AlexNet (2012) was trained on two gaming GPUs. NVIDIA's CUDA software made programming GPUs practical.

events.l: AI data centres with tens of thousands of GPUs

deep.x: Specialised chips
Memory is the bottleneck
Modern AI chips need extremely fast memory (HBM) to feed their cores; memory bandwidth often limits speed more than raw compute.
Training a frontier model can require tens of thousands of GPUs running for months, consuming as much electricity as a small town.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation do?
options: Works out how each weight contributed to the error
quiz.explain: It sends the error backwards so every weight can be adjusted.

quiz.q: A learning rate that is too high causes…
options: Training that jumps around and may never settle
quiz.explain: Big steps overshoot the minimum.

quiz.q: One full pass through the training data is called…
quiz.explain: An epoch is one complete pass; batches are the small chunks within it.

lessons.title: Is the model any good?
lessons.summary: Accuracy, precision, recall and why one number is never enough.

cards.title: Accuracy can lie
cards.text:
If 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that always says "not fraud" is 99% accurate and completely useless.

When one outcome is rare, accuracy hides the failures you care about most.

deep.x: Accuracy is the share of predictions that are correct. With imbalanced classes, it rewards ignoring the rare class. Fraud, defects, diseases and churn are all rare-event problems.

x: 10,000 transactions, 100 fraud
Model always says "OK"
Accuracy = 9,900 ÷ 10,000 = 99%, fraud caught = 0

deep.x: Better choices for rare events

items.b: how many real cases are caught?

deep.x: Balanced accuracy
Balanced accuracy averages the recall of each class, so a model that ignores the rare class scores only 50%.

deep.r: With rare events, 99% can mean useless

deep.x: Always ask: what does a naive model score on this metric?

cards.title: The confusion matrix
cards.text:
Every prediction lands in one of four boxes: true positives (caught), false positives (false alarms), false negatives (missed) and true negatives (correctly ignored).

Most useful metrics are built from these four counts.

deep.x: A confusion matrix tabulates predictions against reality. For a binary problem it has four cells, and nearly every classification metric is derived from them.
Worked example
A fraud model reviews 10,000 transactions with 100 real frauds. It flags 150: 80 real frauds and 70 false alarms.
Costs differ
Each cell has a business cost or benefit. A missed fraud might cost €500; a false alarm costs a phone call and an annoyed customer, say €5.

x: Missed fraud: 20 × €500 = €10,000
False alarms: 70 × €5 = €350
Total error cost: €10,350

deep.x: Multi-class
With many classes, the matrix grows to show which classes are confused with which: e.g. a document classifier mixing up "invoice" and "credit note".
Look at the confusion matrix before any single summary number.

cards.title: Precision
cards.text: Of everything the model flagged, how much was right? High precision means few false alarms.

deep.x: Precision answers: when the model raises an alert, how often is it right? It matters when false alarms are expensive or erode trust.
When precision matters most

items.b: too many false alarms get ignored

deep.x: Alert fatigue
Security and monitoring teams faced with mostly false alarms start ignoring alerts, including real ones. Raising precision can make a system more useful even if it catches slightly less.
In medical screening, precision is called positive predictive value: for rare diseases, even accurate tests can produce more false positives than true ones.

cards.title: Recall
cards.text: Of all the real cases, how many did the model catch? High recall means few misses.

deep.x: Recall, also called sensitivity, answers: of all the real cases, how many did we catch? It matters when misses are dangerous or costly.
When recall matters most

items.b: a missed fault can cause accidents
missing a sanctioned party is illegal

deep.x: Two-stage systems
A common design uses a high-recall first stage to catch almost everything, then a high-precision second stage (another model or humans) to filter false alarms.

steps: Stage 2: precise model or human review

deep.x: Specificity
The counterpart for negatives is specificity: of all genuine negatives, how many were correctly cleared? Medical tests usually report sensitivity and specificity together.
Recall without precision floods teams with work; precision without recall misses the problem. You need both in balance.

cards.title: The precision–recall trade-off
cards.text: Lower the alarm threshold and you catch more (recall up) but raise more false alarms (precision down). Raise it and the opposite happens. Where to set it is a business choice.

deep.x: Most classifiers output a score; you choose a threshold. Moving it trades precision for recall. Plotting the two across thresholds gives a precision–recall curve.
Choosing the threshold
Pick the threshold that minimises expected cost or meets a constraint ("catch at least 90% of fraud" or "no more than 50 alerts a day for the team").
Capacity matters
If a compliance team can review 200 cases a day, the threshold should produce about 200 alerts, ranked by score, regardless of the abstract "best" F1.
ROC curves
ROC curves plot recall against the false-positive rate. For very imbalanced data, precision–recall curves are usually more informative.
The threshold is a business decision, not a technical one; data scientists should present the options, and owners should choose.

cards.title: F1 score
cards.text: F1 combines precision and recall into one number, their harmonic mean. It is high only when both are high.

deep.x: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. Unlike a simple average, it's dragged down by whichever is lower, so a model can't score well by excelling at one and failing at the other.
Harmonic vs simple average
Variants
Limits
F1 ignores true negatives and treats both error types as equally bad. If false negatives cost 100 times more than false positives, a cost-based metric is better.
F1 is a handy summary for comparing models, but business decisions need costs.

cards.title: Errors for numbers

items.b: error as a % of the true value

cards.text: For regression, you measure how far predictions land from reality. MAE is the average absolute error ("off by €8,000 on average"). RMSE punishes big misses more. MAPE gives the error as a percentage.

deep.x: Regression and forecasting use error metrics measured in the target's units or percentages.

items.b: average absolute error, easy to explain
average signed error, systematic over- or under-prediction

deep.x: Example
Actual sales: 100, 120, 80. Forecasts: 110, 100, 90. Errors: 10, −20, 10.
MAPE's trap
MAPE explodes when actual values are near zero (selling 1 unit vs forecasting 3 is a 200% error). Weighted MAPE (WAPE) or MAE are often more robust for intermittent demand.
Bias matters
A forecast can have low average error but systematically under-predict, causing chronic stock-outs. Track bias separately.
In supply chains, forecast accuracy is often reported as 1 − WAPE, e.g. "85% forecast accuracy".

cards.title: Compare against a baseline
cards.text: A forecast with 10% error sounds good until you learn that "same as last week" gets 11%. Always report your model next to a simple baseline and the current human process.

deep.x: A metric only has meaning in comparison. The relevant comparisons are a naive baseline, the current process and the cost of being wrong.
Forecast value added
Supply-chain teams measure "forecast value added": how much each step (statistical model, planner adjustments) improves on the naive forecast. Sometimes manual adjustments make forecasts worse.
Statistical significance
Small improvements may be noise. Test on enough data, across time periods, and check confidence intervals before claiming a win.
If you can't beat "same as last week", don't deploy a complex model.

cards.title: Test like it will be used
cards.text: Evaluate on data that looks like the future: later dates, new customers, other regions. Then keep monitoring after launch, because the real test starts on day one in production.

deep.x: Offline test scores often overestimate real performance. A good evaluation mimics production: same data sources, same timing, same population.

items: Hold out the most recent period
Test on new customers and regions

deep.x: Shadow mode and A/B tests
